claims.claim: The subject is the House Committee on Rules and its control over what reaches the House floor
claims.sourceSpan: Rules and joint rules (other than those relating to the Code of Official Conduct) and the order of business of the House.

claims.claim: The Rules Committee writes the resolution that sets how long a bill is debated and which amendments may be offered
claims.sourceSpan: A special rule (or rule) is a House resolution (H.Res.) that regulates floor consideration of one or more measures identified in its text.

claims.claim: Majority members of the committee are nominated by the Speaker
claims.sourceSpan: Rule 12(b) of the GOP Conference of the 118th Congress (2023-2024) allows the Speaker to nominate the Republican members of the Rules Committee, subject to approval by the full conference. Democrats use the same appointment procedure when serving in the majority.

claims.claim: The full House must adopt each rule by majority vote

claims.claim: It writes the terms on which most major legislation is debated

claims.claim: CRS definition of a special rule, quoted verbatim
claims.sourceSpan: A special rule (or rule) is a House resolution (H.Res.) that regulates floor consideration of one or more measures identified in its text.

claims.claim: The two purposes of a special rule, quoted verbatim
claims.sourceSpan: (1) to enable the House to consider specific measures by granting them privileged status, and (2) to establish the procedural framework for floor consideration of measures brought up under a rule.

claims.claim: A majority of the House with a quorum present must agree to the resolution before privilege attaches
claims.sourceSpan: Before privilege can be conferred on legislation via special rule, a majority of the House (with a quorum present) must first agree to the resolution.

claims.claim: Special rules almost always prevail, usually along party lines, because written to ensure majority support
claims.sourceSpan: Special rules almost always prevail, usually along party lines, largely because they are written in such a way as to ensure majority party support.

claims.claim: Element 1 of a special rule: identify the procedural forum
claims.sourceSpan: the procedural forum the House would use to consider a particular measure
claims.section: R48308, Provisions of a Special Rule

claims.claim: Element 2: allocate general debate time
claims.sourceSpan: allocate time for Members to engage in general debate

claims.claim: Element 3: establish the base text
claims.sourceSpan: establish the base text open for debate and amendment

claims.claim: Element 4: specify the amendment process
claims.sourceSpan: specify the nature of the amendment process (if any)

claims.claim: Element 5: waive the standing rules so points of order cannot be raised
claims.sourceSpan: adjust (or “waive”) the standing rules in whole or in part to negate points of order from being raised

claims.claim: Element 6: provide for the motion to recommit
claims.sourceSpan: provide for the motion to recommit on initial consideration of a bill or joint resolution.

claims.claim: A waiver is the rule adjusting the standing rules in application to the specified measure
claims.sourceSpan: ability to adjust the standing rules of the House in application to the specified measure

claims.claim: Surgical waivers are rare; the blanket waiver is the more common form

claims.claim: A self-executing provision means no separate vote occurs on the amendment
claims.sourceSpan: it means that no separate vote would occur on the amendment(s).

claims.claim: The Rules Committee arranges rule types along an open-to-closed spectrum with standard kinds in between
claims.sourceSpan: Rules are traditionally referred to along a spectrum, where on one end they are open and the other they are closed. While there is wide variation in the middle, there are certain standard kinds of rules.

claims.claim: Open rules definition, quoted verbatim from the committee
claims.sourceSpan: Open Rules —permit the offering of any amendment that otherwise complies with House rules, and allows debate under the 5-minute rule.

claims.claim: CRS: a rule with no amendment limitations beyond the standing rules is an open rule
claims.sourceSpan: that contains no amendment limitations beyond what the standing rules require

claims.claim: CRS calls the fully open rule rare in current practice
claims.sourceSpan: rare in current practice

claims.claim: Modified-open rules operate much like an open rule but restrict the amendment universe (first quoted fragment)
claims.sourceSpan: operate much like an open rule, but have some restriction

claims.claim: The modified-open restriction is a pre-printing requirement or an overall time limit (second quoted fragment)
claims.sourceSpan: either through a pre-printing requirement or an overall time limit on consideration of amendments.

claims.claim: CRS gives the same modified-open test: minimal restrictions but not fully open
claims.sourceSpan: with minimal restrictions on the ability to offer amendments but not fully open

claims.claim: CRS example of a modified-open restriction: pre-printing in the Congressional Record

claims.claim: Such a rule is referred to as modified open
claims.sourceSpan: would be referred to as modified open

claims.claim: Structured rules definition, quoted verbatim from the committee
claims.sourceSpan: Structured Rules —specify that only certain amendments may be considered and specify the time for debate.

claims.claim: Under a structured rule the eligible amendments are those the Rules Committee prints in its report
claims.sourceSpan: created a structured amendment process whereby only those amendments identified by the Rules Committee in its report on the special rule would be eligible to be offered

claims.claim: Closed rules definition, quoted verbatim from the committee
claims.sourceSpan: Closed Rules —effectively eliminate the opportunity to consider amendments, other than those reported by the committee reporting the bill.

claims.claim: CRS formulation of closed rules: prevent any Member from offering an amendment
claims.sourceSpan: prevent any Member from offering an amendment

claims.claim: CRS formulation of structured rules: restrict amendment opportunities in some way
claims.sourceSpan: restrict amendment opportunities in some way

claims.claim: Structured rules restrict but do not block amendments altogether
claims.sourceSpan: but do not block them altogether—are called structured rules

claims.claim: One hour is the standard general-debate limit under a rule
claims.sourceSpan: Most bills brought to the floor under a rule have a one-hour limit on general debate.

claims.claim: Debate time goes to the managers, normally the chair and ranking minority member of the committee(s) of jurisdiction
claims.sourceSpan: in most cases, the chair and ranking minority member of the relevant committee(s) of jurisdiction

claims.claim: Managers yield discrete portions of that time to members on their side of the aisle
claims.sourceSpan: who would be expected to yield discrete portions of that time to Members on their side of the aisle seeking to engage in debate.

claims.claim: H.Res. 260 allocated seven hours across three of five committees

claims.claim: H.Res. 260 was a resolution of the 118th Congress
claims.sourceSpan: H.Res. 260 (118 th Congress) contained typical special rule language

claims.claim: REMOVED, S-RISK (sweep) plus no fetchable authority: "a 13-member standing committee" and "The committee is split 9-to-4 in favor of the majority party." Committee size and party ratio are fixed per Congress by the majority party and the organizing resolution, not by the standing rules, so they carry no durable source; and no fetchable source for the 119th membership was found this session (rules.house.gov/members 404s, clerk.house.gov/Committee 404s, the Congress.gov committee endpoint returns no roster). Both figures are gone rather than restated from an unfetched source.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed): "A modified open rule or structured rule allows only pre-specified amendments, listed by number in the rule." The Rules Committee's own page and CRS R48308 both keep the two categories apart - modified-open still permits amendments generally, subject to a pre-printing requirement or a time limit; only a structured rule limits amendments to a named list. The page now quotes both definitions from both sources and states the distinction explicitly.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed): "Typically one to four hours for major legislation, split equally between the majority and minority managers of the bill." CRS R48308 states the opposite of the range - "Most bills brought to the floor under a rule have a one-hour limit on general debate" - and its own above-typical example (H.Res. 260) is seven hours, not four. The "split equally" sub-claim appears in no source; R48308 says only that managers yield discrete portions to members on their side of the aisle. Replaced with the sourced one-hour standard and the seven-hour counterexample.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep, independently re-confirmed): "the Consent Calendar for very minor legislation" presented as a live bypass. The stored 119th-Congress House Manual carries Sec. 899 as "Former Consent Calendar" with a cross-reference to the 111th Congress rule. The page now states that the route no longer exists and quotes the Manual. NOTE FOR THE ORCHESTRATOR: the sweep recorded unanimous-consent.html as carrying the identical error; that article was refreshed in the Senate-procedure batch and is outside this batch's file scope.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "If the Rules Committee doesn't act, the bill doesn't come to the floor," stated as an absolute in the lede while the same article described two bypass routes. The page now enumerates four sourced routes that do not require a rule.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "the structural reason it is widely described as an instrument of the majority leadership's agenda rather than an independent legislative body" - characterisation attributed to nobody. Replaced with the sourced appointment practice from R48308 fn.5.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "With 435 members, unlimited debate would make governance impossible." The 435 figure appears in no stored source (grepped across all of data/ref-text/), and the causal claim is unsourced. The section now explains the need for special rules from Rule XIV and the CRS privilege framing instead.

REMOVED, U-FLAG: the "traffic cop" nickname and the two paragraphs built on it ("A traffic cop enforces existing rules; the Rules Committee writes the rules anew for each bill"). The label is in no source. The heading now asks why the House needs special rules and answers it from Rule XIV and R48308.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "Discharge petitions rarely succeed because majority members are generally reluctant to undercut their own leadership's scheduling decisions" - a motive claim about named actors with no source. The discharge paragraph now states the rule's mechanics only and links the discharge-petition explainer.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "This asymmetry - tight House floor control, much looser Senate floor control - is one of the structural reasons why the two chambers often operate at different speeds..." Unsourced causal claim. The Senate section now states only the sourced procedural difference.

REMOVED, U-FLAG: "The minority party has essentially no procedural path to force floor consideration..." - contradicted by the article's own material. Rule XIII clause 6(c) protects the Minority Leader's motion to recommit against any rule, and Rule XV clause 2 allows discharge of the Rules Committee itself; both are now stated with receipts.

ADDED from primary source, not in the sweep: the Rule XIII clause 6(a) same-day restriction and its four exceptions, the clause 6(c) motion-to-recommit protection and its Senate-substitute exception, and the clause 4(a)(1)/4(a)(2)(A) interaction that exempts Rules Committee resolutions from the 72-hour report-availability bar. The pre-refresh article described the committee as unconstrained.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, BLOCKING, adjudicated against hman-119-rule-xv.txt and confirmed): the clause 2(a)(1)(B) quote stopped at "public bill or public resolution" and dropped the trailing restrictive clause "that has been reported by a committee or has been referred to a committee for 30 legislative days." That is a real precondition, not a trim - discharging the Rules Committee is available only where the underlying measure has been reported or has itself sat 30 legislative days in committee. The quote is now complete on the page and on this ledger row.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, BLOCKING, adjudicated and confirmed): the section asserted "Four routes exist" and listed suspension, unanimous consent, inherent privilege and discharge. The same stored Rule XV file carries two more LIVE routes the enumeration excluded - Calendar Wednesday (clause 6, Sec. 900) and the Consensus Calendar (clause 7, Sec. 901a, added in the 116th Congress, 290 cosponsors held for 25 legislative days). Both are now on the page with receipts, the count claim is gone, and the Manual annotation that a bill privileged under the Rules cannot be called up on Calendar Wednesday is quoted, because it is what makes Calendar Wednesday a Rules-Committee bypass.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING): the paraphrase of clause 6(a)(1) said "a two-thirds vote of members voting" and dropped "a quorum being present." The exception is now quoted in full alongside the other three.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NON-BLOCKING x2): the page now states R48308 December 2024 vintage where it reports the party-conference appointment practice, adds that conference rules are readopted each Congress so the rule number is a snapshot, and states CRS 98-225 May 19, 2008 update date in the prose, the Key Sources box and the JSON-LD citation. The two CRS citations are now dated consistently.

ROUND 2 FIX (hostile Sonnet verifier, NOTE): the H.Res. 260 debate-time passage dropped the three committees CRS names. Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure are now on the page.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, BLOCKING, adjudicated against hman-119-rule-xiii.txt and confirmed): the limits section said "Rule XIII binds it in two places" and covered only clause 6(a) and 6(c). The same clause carries three more live constraints - 6(d) (three-legislative-day filing duty, and any committee member may call up a report the filer has left uncalled for seven legislative days), 6(e) (an adverse report on a special-order resolution is callable as a privileged question on the second and fourth Mondays), and 6(g) (the accompanying report must specify waivers of points of order to the maximum extent possible). All three are now on the page and the count claim is gone. Same defect class as the round-2 bypass finding: an explicit count contradicted by the source file the page already cites.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, BLOCKING, adjudicated and confirmed): the Calendar Wednesday quote broke exactly where the rule opens a parenthetical, dropping "(except as provided by clause 4 of rule XIV)" with no ellipsis, and also paraphrased "other member authorized by the committee" as "an authorized member" inside what read as quoted text. Clause 6(a) is now quoted in one unbroken verbatim span, and clause 6(c) (the clause does not apply during the last two weeks of a session) has been added.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): the Consensus Calendar paragraph gave the window, the 290-cosponsor threshold and the 25-legislative-day count but never said the route closes when the committee acts. ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): suspension was described only by clause 1(a). Clause 1(c) (40 minutes of debate, divided equally) and clause 1(b) (only a motion to adjourn may be entertained while a suspension motion is pending) are now on the page - the 40-minute cap being the fact that makes suspension a materially different route from a special rule.

ROUND 3 FIX (hostile Sonnet pass 2, NON-BLOCKING): the discharge paragraph gave only the two routes and the 218 threshold.
